claim: The study assessed structural connectome development in a large longitudinal sample ranging from childhood to young adulthood.
source: Here, we assessed structural connectome development in a large longitudinal sample ranging from childhood to young adulthood.
evidence: The abstract directly states the study design and sample characteristics.

claim: Projecting high-dimensional connectomes into compact manifold spaces identified a marked expansion of structural connectomes during adolescence.
source: By projecting high-dimensional connectomes into compact manifold spaces, we identified a marked expansion of structural connectomes, with strongest effects in transmodal regions during adolescence.
evidence: The abstract reports findings from manifold analysis showing connectome expansion.

claim: The strongest effects of connectome expansion were observed in transmodal regions during adolescence.
source: By projecting high-dimensional connectomes into compact manifold spaces, we identified a marked expansion of structural connectomes, with strongest effects in transmodal regions during adolescence.
evidence: The abstract specifies the regional distribution of the observed effects.

claim: Connectome expansion findings reflected increased within-module connectivity together with increased segregation.
source: Findings reflected increased within-module connectivity together with increased segregation, indicating increasing differentiation of higher-order association networks from the rest of the brain.
evidence: The abstract describes the topological characteristics of the observed connectome changes.

claim: The connectome changes indicate increasing differentiation of higher-order association networks from the rest of the brain.
source: Findings reflected increased within-module connectivity together with increased segregation, indicating increasing differentiation of higher-order association networks from the rest of the brain.
evidence: The abstract provides an interpretation of the topological findings.

claim: Projection of subcortico-cortical connectivity patterns into manifolds showed parallel alterations in pathways centered on the caudate and thalamus.
source: Projection of subcortico-cortical connectivity patterns into these manifolds showed parallel alterations in pathways centered on the caudate and thalamus.
evidence: The abstract reports findings from subcortical connectivity analysis.

claim: Connectome findings were contextualized via spatial transcriptome association analysis, highlighting genes enriched in cortex, thalamus, and striatum.
source: Connectome findings were contextualized via spatial transcriptome association analysis, highlighting genes enriched in cortex, thalamus, and striatum.
evidence: The abstract describes the transcriptomic analysis and its results.

claim: Statistical learning of cortical and subcortical manifold features at baseline and their maturational change predicted measures of intelligence at follow-up.
source: Statistical learning of cortical and subcortical manifold features at baseline and their maturational change predicted measures of intelligence at follow-up.
evidence: The abstract reports the results of machine learning prediction analysis.

claim: Adolescence is a critical time for the continued maturation of brain networks.
source: Adolescence is a critical time for the continued maturation of brain networks.
evidence: The abstract opening statement establishes the developmental context.

claim: Adolescence is a time of profound and genetically mediated changes in whole-brain network organization.
source: Adolescence is a time of profound and genetically mediated changes in whole-brain network organization (Larsen and Luna, 2018; Menon, 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites prior literature to establish the developmental context.

claim: Adolescent development is important for the maturation in cognitive and educational functions and brain health more generally.
source: Adolescent development is important for the maturation in cognitive and educational functions and brain health more generally, a notion reinforced by the overlapping onset of several neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders (Hong et al., 2019; Khundrakpam et al., 2017; Paus et al., 2008).
evidence: The introduction cites literature supporting the importance of adolescent development.

claim: The overlapping onset of several neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders reinforces the importance of adolescent brain development.
source: Adolescent development is important for the maturation in cognitive and educational functions and brain health more generally, a notion reinforced by the overlapping onset of several neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders (Hong et al., 2019; Khundrakpam et al., 2017; Paus et al., 2008).
evidence: The introduction cites literature linking adolescent development to disorder onset.

claim: Several cross-sectional and longitudinal studies in neurodevelopmental cohorts have focused on the analysis of morphological changes.
source: Several cross-sectional and longitudinal studies in neurodevelopmental cohorts have focused on the analysis of morphological changes (Gogtay et al., 2004; Shaw et al., 2006; Tamnes et al., 2017), including MRI-based cortical thickness (Shaw et al., 2006; Tamnes et al., 2017) and volumetric measures (Gogtay et al., 2004; Tamnes et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites prior morphological studies.

claim: Studies robustly show initial gray matter increases until mid-late childhood followed by a decline for the rest of the lifespan.
source: Studies robustly show initial gray matter increases until mid-late childhood followed by a decline for the rest of the lifespan.
evidence: The introduction summarizes findings from prior morphological studies.

claim: During adolescence, cortical thickness decreases in widespread brain regions.
source: During adolescence, cortical thickness decreases in widespread brain regions (Khundrakpam et al., 2013; Shaw et al., 2006; Sotiras et al., 2017; Tamnes et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on cortical thickness changes during adolescence.

claim: More recent work explored changes in intracortical microstructure, capitalizing on myelin-sensitive contrasts such as magnetization transfer ratio (MT) mapping, which generally suggest overall increases in adolescence.
source: More recent work explored changes in intracortical microstructure, capitalizing on myelin-sensitive contrasts such as magnetization transfer ratio (MT) mapping, which generally suggest overall increases in adolescence (Paquola et al., 2019a; Whitaker et al., 2016) together with depth-dependent shifts in intracortical myelin profiles (Paquola et al., 2019a).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on intracortical microstructure changes.

claim: An increasing body of connectome-level studies emphasizes that subcortical structures contribute significantly to patterns of whole-brain organization, dynamics, and cognition.
source: Indeed, an increasing body of connectome-level studies emphasizes that subcortical structures contribute significantly to patterns of whole-brain organization, dynamics, and cognition (Hwang et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2020; Shine et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on the role of subcortical structures.

claim: The volumes of the striatum and thalamus decrease between adolescence and adulthood.
source: In prior neurodevelopmental studies, it has been shown that the volumes of the striatum and thalamus decrease between adolescence and adulthood, potentially paralleling processes resulting in cortical gray matter reduction during this time window (Herting et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on subcortical volume changes.

claim: Cortico-subcortical pathways are intrinsically remodeled during adolescence.
source: A close inter-relationship between cortical and subcortical development is also suggested by recent functional connectivity work suggesting that cortico-subcortical pathways are intrinsically remodeled during adolescence (Váša et al., 2020), and these changes affect cognitive functioning.
evidence: The introduction cites literature on cortico-subcortical pathway remodeling.

claim: Changes in cortico-subcortical pathways affect cognitive functioning.
source: A close inter-relationship between cortical and subcortical development is also suggested by recent functional connectivity work suggesting that cortico-subcortical pathways are intrinsically remodeled during adolescence (Váša et al., 2020), and these changes affect cognitive functioning.
evidence: The introduction cites literature linking pathway changes to cognition.

claim: Prior cross-sectional and longitudinal studies in children and adolescents outlined changes in the microstructure of major white matter tracts during development based on the analysis of dMRI-derived tissue parameters.
source: Prior cross-sectional and longitudinal studies in children and adolescents outlined changes in the microstructure of major white matter tracts during development based on the analysis of dMRI-derived tissue parameters (Lebel and Beaulieu, 2011; Schmithorst and Yuan, 2010).
evidence: The introduction cites prior dMRI studies on white matter development.

claim: Graph-theoretical analysis reported a relatively preserved spatial layout of structural hubs across adolescent development.
source: These findings have been complemented by assessments of brain network topology using graph-theoretical analysis (Baker et al., 2015; Hagmann et al., 2010; Lebel and Beaulieu, 2011; Oldham and Fornito, 2019), which reported a relatively preserved spatial layout of structural hubs across adolescent development on the one hand (Hagmann et al., 2010), yet with a continued strengthening of their connectivity profiles, likely underpinned by the ongoing maturation of long-range association fibers (Baker et al., 2015; Lebel and Beaulieu, 2011; Oldham and Fornito, 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on graph-theoretical findings.

claim: There is a continued strengthening of structural hub connectivity profiles during adolescence, likely underpinned by the ongoing maturation of long-range association fibers.
source: These findings have been complemented by assessments of brain network topology using graph-theoretical analysis (Baker et al., 2015; Hagmann et al., 2010; Lebel and Beaulieu, 2011; Oldham and Fornito, 2019), which reported a relatively preserved spatial layout of structural hubs across adolescent development on the one hand (Hagmann et al., 2010), yet with a continued strengthening of their connectivity profiles, likely underpinned by the ongoing maturation of long-range association fibers (Baker et al., 2015; Lebel and Beaulieu, 2011; Oldham and Fornito, 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on connectivity strengthening and its potential mechanism.

claim: Manifold learning techniques decompose whole-brain structural and functional connectomes into a series of lower dimensional axes capturing spatial gradients of connectivity variations.
source: By decomposing whole-brain structural and functional connectomes into a series of lower dimensional axes capturing spatial gradients of connectivity variations, these techniques provide a compact perspective on large-scale connectome organization (Margulies et al., 2016; Paquola et al., 2019b; Vos de Wael et al., 2020a).
evidence: The introduction describes the manifold learning approach with citations.

claim: Manifold learning techniques provide a compact perspective on large-scale connectome organization.
source: By decomposing whole-brain structural and functional connectomes into a series of lower dimensional axes capturing spatial gradients of connectivity variations, these techniques provide a compact perspective on large-scale connectome organization (Margulies et al., 2016; Paquola et al., 2019b; Vos de Wael et al., 2020a).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on the utility of manifold learning.

claim: Multiple dMRI gradients can illustrate structural underpinnings of dynamic functional communication in the adult human connectome.
source: In prior work, we showed that multiple dMRI gradients can illustrate structural underpinnings of dynamic functional communication in the adult human connectome (Park et al., 2021b).
evidence: The introduction cites the authors' prior work on dMRI gradients.

claim: The principal gradients estimated from resting-state functional, microstructural, and diffusion MRI all converge broadly along an established model of sensory-fugal hierarchy and laminar differentiation.
source: Beyond these methodological considerations, prior work has shown that the principal gradients estimated from resting-state functional (Margulies et al., 2016), microstructural (Paquola et al., 2019b), and diffusion MRI (Park et al., 2021a) all converge broadly along an established model of sensory-fugal hierarchy and laminar differentiation (Mesulam, 1998), allowing gradient mapping techniques to make conceptual contact to theories of cortical organization, development, and evolution (Buckner and Krienen, 2013; Goulas et al., 2018; Huntenburg et al., 2018; Sanides, 1969; Sanides, 1962).
evidence: The introduction cites literature showing convergence of gradient findings with hierarchical models.

claim: Gradient mapping techniques allow conceptual contact to theories of cortical organization, development, and evolution.
source: Beyond these methodological considerations, prior work has shown that the principal gradients estimated from resting-state functional (Margulies et al., 2016), microstructural (Paquola et al., 2019b), and diffusion MRI (Park et al., 2021a) all converge broadly along an established model of sensory-fugal hierarchy and laminar differentiation (Mesulam, 1998), allowing gradient mapping techniques to make conceptual contact to theories of cortical organization, development, and evolution (Buckner and Krienen, 2013; Goulas et al., 2018; Huntenburg et al., 2018; Sanides, 1969; Sanides, 1962).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on the theoretical utility of gradient mapping.

claim: The gradient framework has shown utility to study primate evolution and cross-species alignment.
source: An emerging literature has indeed shown utility of the gradient framework to study primate evolution and cross-species alignment (Blazquez Freches et al., 2020; Valk et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2020), neurodevelopment (Hong et al., 2019; Paquola et al., 2019a), as well as plasticity and structure-function coupling (Park et al., 2021b; Valk Sofie et al., 2020; Vázquez-Rodríguez et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on applications of the gradient framework.

claim: Manifold learning techniques applied to myelin sensitive intracortical MT data showed an increasing myeloarchitectural differentiation of association cortex throughout adolescence.
source: In a recent assessment by our team, manifold learning techniques have been applied to myelin sensitive intracortical MT data, showing an increasing myeloarchitectural differentiation of association cortex throughout adolescence (Paquola et al., 2019a).
evidence: The introduction cites the authors' prior work on myeloarchitectural differentiation.

claim: The longitudinal maturation of dMRI connectomes in children and adolescents using manifold techniques has not been tracked.
source: Still, the longitudinal maturation of dMRI connectomes in children and adolescents using manifold techniques has not been tracked.
evidence: The introduction identifies a gap in the literature.

claim: The Allen Human Brain Atlas can be utilized to spatially associate macroscale imaging/connectome data with the expression patterns of thousands of genes.
source: Recently established resources, such as the Allen Human Brain Atlas (Arnatkeviciute et al., 2019; Hawrylycz et al., 2015), can be utilized to spatially associate macroscale imaging/connectome data with the expression patterns of thousands of genes.
evidence: The introduction cites the Allen Human Brain Atlas as a resource.

claim: Studies in newborns have shown that cortical morphology reflects spatiotemporal patterns of gene expression in fetuses.
source: For example, studies in newborns have shown that cortical morphology reflects spatiotemporal patterns of gene expression in fetuses, linking molecular mechanisms to in vivo measures of cortical development in early life (Ball et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on gene expression and cortical morphology in newborns.

claim: Developmental changes in regional cortical thickness measures and myelin proxies spatially co-localize with the expression patterns of genes involved in synaptic and oligodendroglial function.
source: Work in adolescents has furthermore shown that developmental changes in regional cortical thickness measures and myelin proxies spatially co-localize with the expression patterns of genes involved in synaptic and oligodendroglial function (Paquola et al., 2019a; Whitaker et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on gene expression patterns in adolescents.

claim: The study charted developmental changes in structural connectome organization based on an accelerated longitudinal neuroimaging study involving 208 participants investigated between 14 and 26 years of age.
source: Here, we charted developmental changes in structural connectome organization, based on an accelerated longitudinal neuroimaging study involving 208 participants investigated between 14 and 26 years of age (Kiddle et al., 2018; Whitaker et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction describes the study design and sample.

claim: Longitudinal studies track within-subject change, separating developmental effects from between-subject variability.
source: Compared to cross-sectional designs, longitudinal studies track within-subject change, separating developmental effects from between-subject variability (Louis et al., 1986).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on the advantages of longitudinal designs.

claim: IQ is a widely used marker of general cognitive abilities, which shows good test–retest reliability.
source: IQ is a widely used marker of general cognitive abilities, which shows good test–retest reliability (Brown and May, 1979; Watkins and Smith, 2013; Catron, 1978; G.-Matarazzo et al., 1973; Snow et al., 1989; Wagner and Caldwell, 1979) and has previously been applied to index overall cognitive function during development (Crespi, 2016; Garde et al., 2005; Garde et al., 2000; Koenis et al., 2018; Park et al., 2016; Ramsden et al., 2011; Shaw et al., 2006; Suprano et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on IQ as a cognitive measure.

claim: The study included 208 healthy individuals enrolled in an accelerated longitudinal study.
source: In brief, we studied 208 healthy individuals enrolled in an accelerated longitudinal study, with approximately equal numbers of males and females in each of five age-related strata that collectively spanned the time period from 14 to 25 years coinciding with transition from adolescence to young adulthood.
evidence: The Results section describes the study sample.

claim: Participants had approximately equal numbers of males and females in each of five age-related strata.
source: In brief, we studied 208 healthy individuals enrolled in an accelerated longitudinal study, with approximately equal numbers of males and females in each of five age-related strata that collectively spanned the time period from 14 to 25 years coinciding with transition from adolescence to young adulthood.
evidence: The Results section describes the sample stratification.

claim: Participants were 48% female with a mean age of 18.82 years (range = 14–25 years) at baseline and 19.95 years (15–26 years) at follow-up.
source: Participants (48% female) had a mean age of 18.82 years (range = 14–25 years) at baseline and 19.95 years (15–26 years) at follow-up.
evidence: The Results section provides demographic information.

claim: The average interval between baseline and follow-up scan was 11.28 months (range = 6–12 months).
source: The average interval between baseline and follow-up scan was 11.28 months (range = 6–12 months).
evidence: The Results section describes the scan interval.

claim: Three eigenvectors (E1, E2, and E3) explained approximately 50% of information in the template affinity matrix.
source: Three eigenvectors (E1, E2, and E3) explained approximately 50% of information in the template affinity matrix (i.e., 20.7/15.8/13.5% for E1/E2/E3, respectively), with each eigenvector showing a different axis of spatial variation across the cortical mantle (Figure 1A).
evidence: The Results section reports the variance explained by eigenvectors, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Each eigenvector showed a different axis of spatial variation across the cortical mantle.
source: Three eigenvectors (E1, E2, and E3) explained approximately 50% of information in the template affinity matrix (i.e., 20.7/15.8/13.5% for E1/E2/E3, respectively), with each eigenvector showing a different axis of spatial variation across the cortical mantle (Figure 1A).
evidence: The Results section describes the spatial patterns of eigenvectors, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Eigenvectors depicted a continuous differentiation between medial and lateral cortices (E1), between inferior and superior cortices (E2), and between anterior and posterior areas (E3).
source: Eigenvectors depicted a continuous differentiation between medial and lateral cortices (E1), between inferior and superior cortices (E2), and between anterior and posterior areas (E3).
evidence: The Results section describes the spatial patterns of each eigenvector.

claim: The manifold eccentricity showed high values in frontal and somatomotor regions, while temporoparietal, visual, and limbic regions showed low values.
source: The manifold eccentricity showed high values in frontal and somatomotor regions, while temporoparietal, visual, and limbic regions showed low values (Figure 1B).
evidence: The Results section describes the spatial distribution of manifold eccentricity, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Manifold eccentricity expanded as age increased, especially in bilateral prefrontal and temporal areas, as well as left early visual and right lateral parietal cortices.
source: Manifold eccentricity expanded as age increased, especially in bilateral prefrontal and temporal areas, as well as left early visual and right lateral parietal cortices (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.05; Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995; Figure 1C).
evidence: The Results section reports age-related changes in manifold eccentricity, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Peak effects of manifold eccentricity expansion were identified in heteromodal association and paralimbic areas.
source: Stratifying these effects along four cortical hierarchical levels, defined using an established taxonomy based on patterns of laminar differentiation and tract-tracing data in non-human primates (Mesulam, 1998), we identified peak effects in heteromodal association and paralimbic areas (Figure 1D).
evidence: The Results section reports stratified findings by cortical hierarchy, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Highest effects of manifold eccentricity expansion were observed in default mode and limbic areas followed by visual and frontoparietal cortices when analyzed with respect to intrinsic functional communities.
source: Convergent findings were observed when analyzing the effects with respect to intrinsic functional communities (Yeo et al., 2011), showing highest effects in default mode and limbic areas followed by visual and frontoparietal cortices.
evidence: The Results section reports stratified findings by functional communities.

claim: No significant contraction of manifold eccentricity was observed.
source: No significant contraction of manifold eccentricity was observed.
evidence: The Results section reports the absence of contraction effects.

claim: No significant effects were found when fitting the model with a quadratic form of age, indicating the manifold eccentricity linearly increases across age.
source: In addition, we could not find any significant effects when we fitted the model with a quadratic form of age (i.e., age2), indicating the manifold eccentricity linearly increases across age.
evidence: The Results section reports the absence of quadratic age effects.

claim: Significant positive associations were found between manifold eccentricity changes and degree centrality and within-module degree.
source: We found significant positive associations for degree centrality and within-module degree, suggesting that connectome manifold expansion reflects a concurrent increase of overall connectivity, particularly within modules.
evidence: The Results section reports correlations with graph-theoretical measures, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Connectome manifold expansion reflects a concurrent increase of overall connectivity, particularly within modules.
source: We found significant positive associations for degree centrality and within-module degree, suggesting that connectome manifold expansion reflects a concurrent increase of overall connectivity, particularly within modules.
evidence: The Results section provides an interpretation of the correlation findings.

claim: The study replicated findings showing cortical thinning in almost all brain regions across the studied age window.
source: We replicated these findings by showing cortical thinning in almost all brain regions across the studied age window as well as reductions in depth-dependent MT skewness, suggestive of supragranular enrichment of myelin (Figure 2A).
evidence: The Results section reports replication of prior morphological findings, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: The study found reductions in depth-dependent MT skewness, suggestive of supragranular enrichment of myelin.
source: We replicated these findings by showing cortical thinning in almost all brain regions across the studied age window as well as reductions in depth-dependent MT skewness, suggestive of supragranular enrichment of myelin (Figure 2A).
evidence: The Results section reports MT findings, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Virtually identical spatial patterns of manifold eccentricity changes were observed in models that controlled for thickness, MT skewness, and both.
source: While we observed virtually identical spatial patterns of manifold eccentricity changes in models that controlled for thickness, MT skewness, and both, age-related effects in regions of significant manifold eccentricity findings (see Figure 1C) were reduced in models that additionally controlled for these covariates (average reduction of t-value in models controlling for thickness/MT skewness/both = 42/18/68%).
evidence: The Results section reports findings from models controlling for morphological measures, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Age-related effects in regions of significant manifold eccentricity findings were reduced in models that additionally controlled for thickness and MT covariates.
source: While we observed virtually identical spatial patterns of manifold eccentricity changes in models that controlled for thickness, MT skewness, and both, age-related effects in regions of significant manifold eccentricity findings (see Figure 1C) were reduced in models that additionally controlled for these covariates (average reduction of t-value in models controlling for thickness/MT skewness/both = 42/18/68%).
evidence: The Results section reports the reduction in effect sizes after controlling for covariates.

claim: The caudate and thalamus showed significant age-related effects on subcortical-weighted manifolds after multiple comparisons correction.
source: After multiple comparisons correction, the caudate and thalamus showed significant age-related effects on subcortical-weighted manifolds (FDR < 0.05; Figure 3), and marginal effects were observed in the putamen, pallidum, and hippocampus (FDR < 0.1).
evidence: The Results section reports subcortical findings, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Marginal age-related effects on subcortical-weighted manifolds were observed in the putamen, pallidum, and hippocampus.
source: After multiple comparisons correction, the caudate and thalamus showed significant age-related effects on subcortical-weighted manifolds (FDR < 0.05; Figure 3), and marginal effects were observed in the putamen, pallidum, and hippocampus (FDR < 0.1).
evidence: The Results section reports marginal subcortical findings, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Marked expression of genes was found enriched from childhood onward in the cortex, thalamus, and cerebellum.
source: We found marked expression of the genes enriched from childhood onward in the cortex, thalamus, and cerebellum (FDR < 0.001; Figure 4B).
evidence: The Results section reports developmental enrichment findings, with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Genes were enriched for expression in the striatum at the transition from childhood to adolescence, although signal was reduced.
source: Although signal was reduced, genes were also enriched for expression in the striatum at the transition from childhood to adolescence (FDR < 0.05).
evidence: The Results section reports striatal gene enrichment findings.

claim: Identified genes were not found to be expressed in the hippocampus and amygdala.
source: On the other hand, identified genes were not found to be expressed in the hippocampus and amygdala.
evidence: The Results section reports the absence of gene expression in specific regions.

claim: The manifold eccentricity of cortical regions at baseline significantly predicted future IQ score.
source: The manifold eccentricity of cortical regions at baseline significantly predicted future IQ score (mean ± SD r = 0.14 ± 0.04; mean absolute error [MAE] = 8.93 ± 0.16, p=0.09).
evidence: The Results section reports IQ prediction results.

claim: Prediction performance was slightly improved when combining the manifold eccentricity both at baseline and differences between follow-up and baseline.
source: Prediction performance was slightly improved when we combined the manifold eccentricity both at baseline and differences between follow-up and baseline (r = 0.18 ± 0.04; MAE = 9.10 ± 0.19, p=0.04) (Figure 5A).
evidence: The Results section reports improved prediction with trajectory data, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Prediction accuracy was improved if subcortical manifold features were additionally considered.
source: Notably, prediction accuracy was improved if we additionally considered subcortical manifold features (baseline: r = 0.17 ± 0.03; MAE = 8.74 ± 0.11, p=0.04; baseline and maturational change: r = 0.21 ± 0.02; MAE = 8.86 ± 0.14, p=0.01) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The Results section reports improved prediction with subcortical features, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: The regions showing strongest predictive validity for IQ were prefrontal, parietal, and temporal cortices, as well as the caudate and thalamus.
source: The regions showing strongest predictive validity for IQ were prefrontal, parietal, and temporal cortices, as well as the caudate and thalamus.
evidence: The Results section identifies regions with high predictive validity.

claim: The prediction model outperformed a baseline model where IQ of the test set was simple average of training set.
source: We compared the prediction performance of our model with a baseline model, where IQ of the test set was simple average of training set (r = −0.15 ± 0.06, MAE = 8.98 ± 0.04, p=0.12; see Materials and methods). We found that our model outperformed this baseline model (Meng's z-test p < 0.001) (Meng et al., 1992).
evidence: The Results section reports comparison with a baseline model.

claim: No significant results were found when predicting the change of IQ between the baseline and follow-up.
source: We also predicted the change of IQ between the baseline and follow-up, instead of IQ at follow-up, using the imaging features. However, we could not find significant results.
evidence: The Results section reports the absence of significant findings for IQ change prediction.

claim: Findings were highly consistent when repeating the longitudinal modeling with a different spatial scale (300 parcels).
source: Repeating the longitudinal modeling with a different spatial scale (i.e., 300 parcels), findings were highly consistent (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The Results section reports sensitivity analysis with different parcellation, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Manifold eccentricity of the identified cortical regions and age consistently correlated positively across different sites and within both biological sexes, yielding non-significant interaction effects.
source: Furthermore, manifold eccentricity of the identified cortical regions and age consistently correlated positively across different sites and within both biological sexes, yielding non-significant interaction effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The Results section reports site and sex sensitivity analysis, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: T-statistic maps of age-related changes in manifold eccentricity were largely consistent when changing parameters of diffusion map embedding.
source: When we changed parameters of diffusion map embedding for generating connectome manifolds (see Materials and methods), t-statistic maps of age-related changes in manifold eccentricity were largely consistent (mean ± SD linear correlation r = 0.92 ± 0.10).
evidence: The Results section reports sensitivity analysis with different embedding parameters.

claim: Significant increases in alignment were found after Procrustes alignment compared to before alignment.
source: When calculating linear correlations between template and individual manifolds before and after alignment, we found significant increases after alignment (r = 0.92 ± 0.03/0.93 ± 0.03/0.94 ± 0.03) compared to before alignment (−0.02 ± 0.03/–0.001 ± 0.37/0.003 ± 0.12) for E1/E2/E3, respectively, supporting effectiveness of alignment.
evidence: The Results section reports alignment quality assessment.

claim: Consistent age-related changes in manifold eccentricity were found after excluding 10% of subjects with poor alignment.
source: After excluding 10% of subjects with poor alignment (cutoff r = 0.83; the new set was correlated with the template manifold, r = 0.94 ± 0.01), we found consistent age-related changes in manifold eccentricity (Figure 1—figure supplement 6), with the t-statistic map showing strong correlation to the map derived in the whole sample (r = 0.97, p<0.001).
evidence: The Results section reports sensitivity analysis excluding poorly aligned subjects, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Consistent spatial maps and longitudinal findings were found when generating eigenvectors using principal component analysis instead of diffusion map embedding.
source: In a separate analysis, we generated eigenvectors using principal component analysis (Wold et al., 1987), instead of diffusion map embedding (Coifman and Lafon, 2006), and found consistent spatial maps (linear correlation = 0.998 ± 0.001 across E1/E2/E3; Figure 1—figure supplement 7A) and longitudinal findings (Figure 1—figure supplement 7B).
evidence: The Results section reports sensitivity analysis with different dimensionality reduction method, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: Significant age-related longitudinal changes were found in degree and eigenvector centrality, while betweenness centrality did not reveal significant effects.
source: Repeating the longitudinal modeling using graph-theoretical centrality measures, we found significant age-related longitudinal changes in degree and eigenvector centrality, while betweenness centrality did not reveal significant effects, in similar regions to those that had significant age-related changes in manifold eccentricity (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: The Results section reports sensitivity analysis with graph-theoretical measures, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: Significant yet variable spatial similarity was found between effect size maps for manifold eccentricity and each graph measure.
source: Correlating the effect size maps for manifold eccentricity and each graph measure, we found a significant yet variable spatial similarity of the effect maps (betweenness centrality: r = 0.18, spin-test p = 0.02; degree centrality: r = 0.57, p < 0.001; eigenvector centrality: r = 0.47, p < 0.001).
evidence: The Results section reports spatial correlations between manifold and graph measures.

claim: Relatively consistent results with original findings were observed when repeating manifold eccentricity calculation using all eigenvectors instead of only the first three.
source: Repeating manifold eccentricity calculation and age modeling using all eigenvectors, instead of using only the first three, we observed relatively consistent results with our original findings (linear correlation of manifold eccentricity r = 0.54, p<0.001; t-statistic map r = 0.68, p<0.001), also pointing to manifold expansion in transmodal cortices (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: The Results section reports sensitivity analysis using all eigenvectors, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 9.

claim: High similarity in spatial maps of the estimated manifolds was found when comparing gradients derived from different thresholding approaches.
source: We compared gradients derived from the group representative structural connectome, based on (i) distance-dependent thresholding (Betzel et al., 2019) and (ii) consistency thresholding (Wang et al., 2019; Figure 1—figure supplement 10). We found high similarity in spatial maps of the estimated manifolds (r = 0.89 ± 0.01 for E1; 0.93 ± 0.004 for E2; 0.85 ± 0.01 for E3 across six different thresholds), indicating robustness.
evidence: The Results section reports sensitivity analysis with different thresholding approaches, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 10.

claim: Strong age-related effects in heteromodal association areas were replicated using a structural parcellation scheme, together with effects in caudate and hippocampus.
source: We repeated our analyses with a structural parcellation, defined using a sub-parcellation of folding based on the Desikan–Killiany atlas (Desikan et al., 2006; Vos de Wael et al., 2020a; Figure 1—figure supplement 11). Despite slight differences in the topography of manifold eccentricity in lateral prefrontal, temporal, and occipital cortices, we could replicate strong age-related effects in heteromodal association areas, together with effects in caudate and hippocampus (FDR < 0.05), and marginally in thalamus (FDR < 0.1).
evidence: The Results section reports sensitivity analysis with structural parcellation, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 11.

claim: Significant increases in edge weights were found within frontoparietal and default mode networks, as well as in attention and sensory networks when repeating the longitudinal modeling using connectome edge weights.
source: Repeating the longitudinal modeling across age using connectome edge weights, we found significant increases in edge weights within frontoparietal and default mode networks, as well as in attention and sensory networks (FDR < 0.05; Figure 1—figure supplement 12), consistent with findings based on manifold eccentricity.
evidence: The Results section reports sensitivity analysis using edge weights, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 12.

claim: Relatively consistent albeit weaker age-related changes in manifold eccentricity were found when repeating the longitudinal modeling within a subset of participants who completed the Tanner scale.
source: We repeated the longitudinal modeling within a subset of participants who completed the Tanner scale (n = 73) (Marshall and Tanner, 1970; Marshall and Tanner, 1969) and found relatively consistent albeit weaker age-related changes in manifold eccentricity as for the overall sample (Figure 1—figure supplement 13A).
evidence: The Results section reports sensitivity analysis with Tanner scale subset, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 13A.

claim: Manifold eccentricity and Tanner scale revealed a significant interaction effect, suggesting that participants in early pubertal stages show more marked changes in manifold eccentricity across age compared to those in later stages.
source: Notably, manifold eccentricity within the identified regions derived from overall sample and Tanner scale revealed a significant interaction effect (t = 2.36, p=0.01; Figure 1—figure supplement 13B), suggesting that participants in early pubertal stages show more marked changes in manifold eccentricity across age compared to those in later stages.
evidence: The Results section reports interaction with pubertal stage, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 13B.

claim: No improved prediction performance was found when predicting IQ at follow-up using a regression tree method instead of linear regression model.
source: We predicted IQ at follow-up using a regression tree method (Breiman et al., 1984), instead of linear regression model, but we could not find improved prediction performance (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The Results section reports sensitivity analysis with nonlinear prediction model, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Higher-order association cortices in prefrontal, medial and superior temporal areas, as well as parieto-occipital regions, expanded in their connectome manifold representation indicative of an increased differentiation of these systems from the rest of the brain in adolescence.
source: Capitalizing on advanced manifold learning techniques applied to dMRI-derived connectomes, we established that higher-order association cortices in prefrontal, medial and superior temporal areas, as well as parieto-occipital regions, expanded in their connectome manifold representation indicative of an increased differentiation of these systems from the rest of the brain in adolescence.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the main findings.

claim: Parallel topological analysis based on graph theory indicated that manifold expansion anatomically coincided with increases in the within-module connectivity of transmodal cortices.
source: Parallel topological analysis based on graph theory indicated that these changes anatomically coincided with increases in the within-module connectivity of transmodal cortices.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the graph-theoretical findings.

claim: Findings were consistent across the different acquisition sites and biological sexes.
source: Findings were consistent across the different acquisition sites and biological sexes, and similar albeit slightly weaker when correcting connectivity manifolds for MRI-based measures of macrostructure (cortical thickness) and microstructure (skewness of MT depth profile).
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the robustness of findings.

claim: Findings were similar albeit slightly weaker when correcting connectivity manifolds for MRI-based measures of macrostructure and microstructure.
source: Findings were consistent across the different acquisition sites and biological sexes, and similar albeit slightly weaker when correcting connectivity manifolds for MRI-based measures of macrostructure (cortical thickness) and microstructure (skewness of MT depth profile).
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the findings after controlling for morphological measures.

claim: Parallel reconfigurations of subcortical connectivity patterns were found for the caudate and thalamus in addition to the cortical manifold expansion.
source: In addition to the cortical manifold expansion, we found parallel reconfigurations of subcortical connectivity patterns for the caudate and thalamus.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the subcortical findings.

claim: Decoding findings with post-mortem gene expression maps implicated genes enriched in adolescence and young adulthood, pointing to both cortical as well as subcortical targets.
source: Decoding our findings with post-mortem gene expression maps implicated genes enriched in adolescence and young adulthood, again pointing to both cortical as well as subcortical targets.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the transcriptomic findings.

claim: The combination of both cortical and subcortical manifold measures predicted behavioral measures of intelligence at follow-up, with higher performance than cortical or subcortical data alone.
source: Finally, the combination of both cortical and subcortical manifold measures predicted behavioral measures of intelligence at follow-up, with higher performance than cortical or subcortical data alone.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the prediction findings.

claim: Manifold learning offers a low-dimensional perspective on connectome reconfigurations in a data-driven and spatially unconstrained manner.
source: These techniques are appealing as they offer a low-dimensional perspective on connectome reconfigurations in a data-driven and spatially unconstrained manner.
evidence: The Discussion explains the advantages of manifold learning.

claim: Marked connectome expansion during adolescence mainly encompassed transmodal and heteromodal association cortex in prefrontal, temporal, and posterior regions, the territories known to mature later in development.
source: In our longitudinal study, we could identify marked connectome expansion during adolescence, mainly encompassing transmodal and heteromodal association cortex in prefrontal, temporal, and posterior regions, the territories known to mature later in development (Gogtay et al., 2004; Shaw et al., 2006).
evidence: The Discussion interprets the findings in the context of prior literature.

claim: Connectome expansion can be understood as an overall greater differentiation of the connectivity of higher-order areas from the rest of the brain as they would then cover wider portions of the corresponding manifold space.
source: Connectome expansion can be understood as an overall greater differentiation of the connectivity of these areas from the rest of the brain as they would then cover wider portions of the corresponding manifold space.
evidence: The Discussion provides an interpretation of connectome expansion.

claim: Manifold expansion in higher-order areas correlated with an increase in their within-module connectivity, but not with participation coefficient and connectivity distance measures that would be more reflective of their between-module connectivity.
source: Manifold expansion in higher-order areas correlated with an increase in their within-module connectivity, but not with participation coefficient and connectivity distance measures that would be more reflective of their between-module connectivity.
evidence: The Discussion interprets the graph-theoretical correlations.

claim: Macroscale manifold findings likely reflect an ongoing consolidation of transmodal cortical communities.
source: In this context, our macroscale manifold findings likely reflect an ongoing consolidation of transmodal cortical communities.
evidence: The Discussion provides an interpretation of the findings.

claim: These network effects are likely driven by the ongoing maturation of fiber bundles that interconnect higher-order cortices, including superior longitudinal fascicules, but also thalamic and basal ganglia pathways, throughout adolescence.
source: Considering their distributed regional substrate, these network effects are likely driven by the ongoing maturation of fiber bundles that interconnect these higher-order cortices, including superior longitudinal fascicules, but also thalamic and basal ganglia pathways (Tamnes et al., 2010), throughout adolescence.
evidence: The Discussion provides a mechanistic interpretation with citation.

claim: Longitudinal changes in cortical features were overall in agreement with prior work, suggesting marked reductions in cortical thickness in adolescence, possibly reflecting synaptic pruning processes.
source: Longitudinal changes in these cortical features were overall in agreement with prior work, suggesting marked reductions in cortical thickness in adolescence (Khundrakpam et al., 2017; Shaw et al., 2006), possibly reflecting synaptic pruning processes (Petanjek et al., 2011) together with decreases in the skewness of intracortical MT profiles, a feature sensitive to preferential myelination of supragranular layers (Paquola et al., 2019a).
evidence: The Discussion interprets morphological findings in the context of prior literature.

claim: The effect sizes of manifold eccentricity findings were reduced when controlling for intracortical and morphological measures, particularly when controlling for depth-dependent shifts in cortical microstructure.
source: Although we still observed significant age-related changes in manifold eccentricity after controlling for these intracortical and morphological measures, the effect sizes of our findings were reduced. This effect was particularly evident when running a parallel analysis that additionally controlled for depth-dependent shifts in cortical microstructure, a finding in line with more generally demonstrated links between cortical microstructural depth profiles and inter-regional connectivity (Paquola et al., 2019b).
evidence: The Discussion interprets the covariate analysis findings.

claim: Results suggest a coupled process that affects depth-dependent shifts in cortical myeloarchitecture and adolescent shifts in macroscale connectome organization.
source: In the context of adolescence and prior findings in the NSPN dataset (Paquola et al., 2019a), these results thus suggest a coupled process that affects depth-dependent shifts in cortical myeloarchitecture, on the one hand, and adolescent shifts in macroscale connectome organization, on the other hand, as shown by our longitudinal manifold analyses.
evidence: The Discussion provides an interpretation of the coupled processes.

claim: The caudate nucleus of the striatum has long been recognized to play an important role in mediating large-scale cortical network organization.
source: The caudate nucleus of the striatum has long been recognized to play an important role in mediating large-scale cortical network organization (Aglioti, 1997; Alexander and Crutcher, 1990; Graybiel, 1995), a finding also increasingly recognized in the connectome literature (Hwang et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2020; Shine et al., 2019).
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on the role of the caudate.

claim: The caudate is known to modulate activity in prefrontal association areas during memory-driven internal thought processes.
source: It is known to modulate activity in prefrontal association areas during memory-driven internal thought processes (Aglioti, 1997), and higher-order cognitive functions, notably motivational processes, decision making, as well as cognitive control and executive functions more generally (Aglioti, 1997; Graybiel, 1995).
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on caudate function.

claim: Regions of the striatum participate in dense cortico-subcortical feedback loops and exchange neural activity through dense connections with adjacent basal ganglia structures as well as the thalamus.
source: Regions of the striatum participate in dense cortico-subcortical feedback loops and exchange neural activity through dense connections with adjacent basal ganglia structures as well as the thalamus (Aglioti, 1997; Alexander and Crutcher, 1990; Shine, 2021).
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on striatal connectivity.

claim: Coupled network and molecular changes may ultimately change subcortical and cortical circuit properties, including the balance of excitation and inhibition.
source: Coupled network and molecular changes may ultimately change subcortical and cortical circuit properties, including the balance of excitation and inhibition (E/I).
evidence: The Discussion provides a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Human brain development involves spatio-temporal waves of gene expression changes across different brain regions and developmental time windows.
source: Human brain development involves spatio-temporal waves of gene expression changes across different brain regions and developmental time windows (Ip et al., 2010; Kang et al., 2011; Shin et al., 2018).
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on developmental gene expression.

claim: Prior studies have suggested shifts in E/I balance, evolving from a dominant inhibitory bias in early developmental stages towards stronger excitatory drive in later stages, and suggested that these may underlie the maturation of cognitive functions such as working memory and executive control.
source: In the study of adolescent development, prior studies have suggested shifts in E/I balance, evolving from a dominant inhibitory bias in early developmental stages towards stronger excitatory drive in later stages, and suggested that these may underlie the maturation of cognitive functions such as working memory and executive control (Dorrn et al., 2010; Lander et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2007).
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on E/I balance in development.

claim: In common neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism, schizophrenia, and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, imbalances in cortical E/I and cortico-subcortical network function have been demonstrated.
source: In common neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism, schizophrenia, and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, imbalances in cortical E/I and cortico-subcortical network function have been demonstrated (Cellot and Cherubini, 2014; Gandal et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2017; Lewis et al., 2005; Nelson and Valakh, 2015; Park et al., 2021a; Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019; Trakoshis et al., 2020), potentially downstream to perturbations of different neurotransmitter systems, such as interneuron-mediated GABA transmission (Bonaventura et al., 2017; Kilb, 2012; Liu et al., 2007; Park et al., 2021a; Silveri et al., 2013; Trakoshis et al., 2020; Tziortzi et al., 2014).
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on E/I imbalances in disorders.

claim: Application of a supervised machine learning framework demonstrated that it is possible to predict inter-individual variations in future IQ from structural connectome manifold data.
source: Application of a supervised machine learning framework with cross-validation and regularization to our cohort demonstrated that it is possible to predict inter-individual variations in future IQ from structural connectome manifold data.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the prediction findings.

claim: These findings complement conceptual accounts linking brain organization to cognitive function and earlier efforts to predict IQ measures from inter-regional measures of connectivity and graph-theoretical indices of network topology.
source: These findings complement conceptual accounts linking brain organization to cognitive function (Margulies et al., 2016; Mesulam, 1998) and earlier efforts to predict IQ measures from inter-regional measures of connectivity and graph-theoretical indices of network topology (Greene et al., 2018).
evidence: The Discussion contextualizes the prediction findings with prior literature.

claim: Evaluations of several feature combinations highlighted that predictive performance was highest when including both baseline and trajectory data, and when complementing cortical and subcortical manifold features.
source: Notably, evaluations of several feature combinations highlighted that predictive performance was highest when including both baseline and trajectory data, and when complementing cortical and subcortical manifold features.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the feature combination findings.

claim: These findings re-emphasize the benefits of incorporating subcortical nodes in the characterization of large-scale cortical network organization and overall cognitive function.
source: These findings re-emphasize the benefits of incorporating subcortical nodes in the characterization of large-scale cortical network organization and overall cognitive function (Alves et al., 2019; Müller et al., 2020; Shine, 2021; Shine et al., 2019).
evidence: The Discussion interprets the findings with citations.

claim: Although the model significantly outperformed a baseline model, the relationship between the actual and predicted IQ scores did not locate on the equality line and the strength of the association was rather weak.
source: Of note, although our model significantly outperformed a baseline model, the relationship between the actual and predicted IQ scores did not locate on the equality line and the strength of the association was rather weak.
evidence: The Discussion acknowledges limitations of the prediction model.

claim: Adolescence is a time characterized by ongoing brain changes, gradually increasing independence from caregivers, accompanied by strong increments in knowledge and our ability to think more abstractly and to cooperate with our peers to achieve common goals.
source: Adolescence is a time characterized by ongoing brain changes (Baum et al., 2020; Gogtay et al., 2004; Larsen and Luna, 2018; Menon, 2013; Shaw et al., 2006), gradually increasing independence from caregivers, accompanied by strong increments in knowledge and our ability to think more abstractly and to cooperate with our peers to achieve common goals.
evidence: The Discussion provides a broader context for adolescent development.

claim: Adolescence is also a sensitive time window for risk taking, the development of addictions, and is associated with high rates of onset of several psychiatric disorders.
source: On the other hand, adolescence is also a sensitive time window for risk taking, the development of addictions, and is associated with high rates of onset of several psychiatric disorders (Hong et al., 2019; Khundrakpam et al., 2017).
evidence: The Discussion cites literature on adolescent vulnerabilities.

claim: The study has shown that structural brain network organization continues to mature significantly during adolescence, with higher-order association cortices in prefrontal and posterior regions especially showing an expansion of their corresponding connectome manifold signature.
source: Our study has shown that structural brain network organization continues to mature significantly during this time period, with higher-order association cortices in prefrontal and posterior regions especially showing an expansion of their corresponding connectome manifold signature.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the main findings.

claim: Findings were related to an increased strengthening of intra-community connectivity as well as cortico-subcortical connectivity to thalamo-striatal regions.
source: Findings were related to an increased strengthening of intra-community connectivity as well as cortico-subcortical connectivity to thalamo-striatal regions.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the connectivity findings.

claim: The framework may be useful to explore multiscale network perturbations in cohorts with a psychiatric diagnosis or those at risk for addiction or atypical neurodevelopment.
source: Although the current work was restricted to a longitudinal sample of typically developing adolescents, our framework may be useful to explore multiscale network perturbations in cohorts with a psychiatric diagnosis or those at risk for addiction or atypical neurodevelopment.
evidence: The Discussion suggests future applications of the framework.

claim: The final sample consisted of a total of 208 participants collected from three different UK sites: Wolfson Brain Imaging Centre and MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit in Cambridge; and University College London.
source: Our final sample consisted of a total of 208 participants (48% female; mean [range] age = 18.82 [14–25] years at baseline and 19.95 [15–26] at follow-up; inter-scan interval of 11.28 [6–12] months), collected from three different UK sites: Wolfson Brain Imaging Centre and MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit in Cambridge; and University College London.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the sample and sites.

claim: The participants were divided into template and non-template cohorts with matched age, sex, and site ratio.
source: We divided the participants into template and non-template cohorts with matched age, sex, and site ratio.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the cohort division.

claim: The template dataset consisted of 30 participants and was used for constructing the group mean template manifold.
source: The template dataset (n = 30; 50% female; mean [range] age = 18.69 [15–24] years at baseline and 19.84 ± 2.66 [16–25] at follow-up) was used for constructing the group mean template manifold and the non-template dataset (n = 178; 47% female; mean [range] age = 18.84 [14–25] years at baseline and 19.97 [15–26] at follow-up) was used for conducting main analyses.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the template dataset.

claim: The non-template dataset consisted of 178 participants and was used for conducting main analyses.
source: The template dataset (n = 30; 50% female; mean [range] age = 18.69 [15–24] years at baseline and 19.84 ± 2.66 [16–25] at follow-up) was used for constructing the group mean template manifold and the non-template dataset (n = 178; 47% female; mean [range] age = 18.84 [14–25] years at baseline and 19.97 [15–26] at follow-up) was used for conducting main analyses.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the non-template dataset.

claim: Changing the template dataset composition did not markedly affect main findings.
source: Of note, changing the template dataset composition did not markedly affect main findings (Figure 1—figure supplement 14).
evidence: The Materials and methods section reports robustness to template selection, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 14.

claim: Imaging data were obtained using Siemens Magnetom TIM Trio 3T scanners.
source: Imaging data were obtained using Siemens Magnetom TIM Trio 3T scanners.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the MRI scanner.

claim: Individual manifolds were aligned to a template manifold estimated from a hold-out dataset.
source: Individual manifolds were aligned to a template manifold estimated from a hold-out dataset (see Materials and methods) (Langs et al., 2015; Vos de Wael et al., 2020a).
evidence: The Results section describes the alignment procedure with citations.

claim: Manifold eccentricity quantifies the changes in eigenvectors between the time points in terms of expansion and contraction instead of comparing multidimensional connectome manifolds.
source: It thus quantifies the changes in eigenvectors between the time points in terms of expansion and contraction instead of comparing multidimensional connectome manifolds (Bethlehem et al., 2020).
evidence: The Results section explains the manifold eccentricity measure with citation.

claim: Manifold eccentricity quantifies global brain organization based in the connectivity space.
source: Thus, manifold eccentricity quantifies global brain organization based in the connectivity space.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explains the interpretation of manifold eccentricity.
